topic: Struck-by hazards: vehicles, equipment and signalling

notes.front: What is the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD), as the construction standards use it?
notes.back: A traffic control manual incorporated by reference into Part 1926; its Part 6 governs flaggers and traffic control devices.
notes.explanation: Part 1926 does not repeat the manual's contents: it lists the 2009 edition as incorporated by reference for the flagging and traffic-control sections.
notes.example: Like a site's own traffic plan for a road job, but a national manual that the construction rules point to instead of writing the details out.
notes.evidence: Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices for Streets and Highways, 2009 Edition, December 2009 (including Revision 1 dated May 2012 and Revision 2 dated May 2012), (‘‘MUTCD’’) IBR approved for §§ 1926.200(g) and 1926.201(a).
introduces: Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices
uses: Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices

notes.front: What is a rollover protective structure (ROPS), and which subpart of Part 1926 sets its requirements?
notes.back: A protective frame on material handling equipment such as scrapers, front-end loaders, dozers and graders; Subpart W sets its requirements.
notes.explanation: Subpart W applies to listed rubber-tired and crawler equipment used in construction work, and the earthmoving rules in 1926.602 point to it for ROPS.
notes.example: Like a roll cage in a rally car, but fitted to a bulldozer or a motor grader on a construction site.
notes.evidence: This subpart applies to the following types of material handling equipment: All rubber-tired, selfpropelled scrapers, rubber-tired frontend loaders, rubber-tired dozers, wheeltype agricultural and industrial tractors, crawler tractors, crawler-type loaders, and motor graders, with or without attachments, that are used in construction work.

notes.front: Employees working where there is a possible danger of head injury from impact, or from falling or flying objects, must be protected by {{c1::protective helmets}}.
notes.explanation: Section 1926.100 also covers the danger of electrical shock and burns to the head, and names the consensus standards the helmets must meet.
notes.evidence: Employees working in areas where there is a possible danger of head injury from impact, or from falling or flying objects, or from electrical shock and burns, shall be protected by protective helmets.

notes.front: A labourer sorts timber at ground level beside a building where roofers work two storeys above and bundles of shingles are sometimes dropped. What does 1926.100 require for the labourer?
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, because the labourer is not working at height
B) Safety glasses with side shields only
C) A protective helmet
D) A hard hat only if the roofers ask for one
notes.back: C: a protective helmet.
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the rule turns on the danger of falling objects, not on the labourer's own height. B addresses eyes, not the head. D is wrong: the rule does not depend on a request.
notes.explanation: Working below where objects may fall is a possible danger of head injury from falling objects, which is the case 1926.100(a) covers.
notes.evidence: Employees working in areas where there is a possible danger of head injury from impact, or from falling or flying objects, or from electrical shock and burns, shall be protected by protective helmets.

notes.front: Signalling by flaggers, including the warning garments flaggers wear, must conform to which document?
notes.back: Part 6 of the MUTCD.
notes.explanation: Section 1926.201(a) sets no flagging details of its own; it incorporates Part 6 of the MUTCD by reference.
notes.evidence: Signaling by flaggers and the use of flaggers, including warning garments worn by flaggers, shall conform to Part 6 of the MUTCD (incorporated by reference, see § 1926.6).

notes.front: A contractor is resurfacing one lane of a county road and assigns a worker to stop and release traffic with a paddle. Where does Part 1926 send the contractor for how the flagger signals and what the flagger wears?
notes.choices:
A) To the contractor's own judgement, as the rule is silent
B) To the head protection rule in 1926.100
C) To Part 6 of the MUTCD
D) To the accident prevention tag rules
notes.back: C: to Part 6 of the MUTCD.
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: 1926.201(a) is not silent; it incorporates the MUTCD. B covers helmets, not flagging. D covers temporary tags on hazards such as defective tools.
notes.explanation: Both the signalling and the flagger's warning garments are governed by Part 6 of the MUTCD under 1926.201(a).
notes.evidence: Signaling by flaggers and the use of flaggers, including warning garments worn by flaggers, shall conform to Part 6 of the MUTCD (incorporated by reference, see § 1926.6).

notes.front: At points of hazard, what must construction areas be posted with, and protected by?
notes.back: Posted with legible traffic control signs; protected by traffic control devices designed and used to Part 6 of the MUTCD.
notes.explanation: Section 1926.200(g) names signs, signals, markings and barricades among the traffic control devices that must conform to Part 6.
notes.evidence: At points of hazard, construction areas shall be posted with legible traffic control signs and protected by traffic control devices. (2) The design and use of all traffic control devices, including signs, signals, markings, barricades, and other devices, for protection of construction workers shall conform to Part 6 of the MUTCD
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.200(g), Traffic control signs and devices, p. 196

notes.front: Under 1926.601, what are the two ways an employer may use motor vehicle equipment that has an obstructed view to the rear?
notes.back: A reverse signal alarm audible above the surrounding noise level; or backing up only when an observer signals it is safe.
notes.explanation: Either condition satisfies 1926.601(b)(4); without one of them, the vehicle may not be used.
notes.evidence: No employer shall use any motor vehicle equipment having an obstructed view to the rear unless: (i) The vehicle has a reverse signal alarm audible above the surrounding noise level or: (ii) The vehicle is backed up only when an observer signals that it is safe to do so.

notes.front: Earthmoving or compacting equipment with an obstructed rear view may be used in reverse gear only with a reverse signal alarm distinguishable from the surrounding noise level, or when {{c1::an employee signals that it is safe to do so}}.
notes.explanation: Section 1926.602(a)(9) applies the same alarm-or-signaller choice to earthmoving and compacting equipment that 1926.601 applies to motor vehicles.
notes.evidence: used in reverse gear unless the equipment has in operation a reverse signal alarm distinguishable from the surrounding noise level or an employee signals that it is safe to do so.

notes.front: A dump truck's rear window is blocked by its load and its reverse alarm has failed. The foreman wants it to keep delivering fill today. Which option meets 1926.601?
notes.choices:
A) Back up slowly with the hazard lights on
B) Sound the horn once before each reverse
C) Keep working, and repair the alarm at the next service
D) Back up only when an observer signals that it is safe
notes.back: D: back up only when an observer signals that it is safe.
notes.choicesExplained: A and B are not among the two permitted conditions. C is wrong: without a working alarm the rule allows backing only on an observer's signal.
notes.explanation: With the alarm out of action, the observer's signal is the only remaining condition under which the truck may back up.
notes.evidence: No employer shall use any motor vehicle equipment having an obstructed view to the rear unless: (i) The vehicle has a reverse signal alarm audible above the surrounding noise level or: (ii) The vehicle is backed up only when an observer signals that it is safe to do so.

notes.front: Which motor vehicles covered by 1926.601 must have seat belts and anchorages installed, and to what standard?
notes.back: All motor vehicles; the belts and anchorages must meet the Department of Transportation's Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards.
notes.explanation: Section 1926.601(b)(9) borrows the Department of Transportation's vehicle standards rather than setting its own.
notes.evidence: Seat belts and anchorages meeting the requirements of 49 CFR part 571 (Department of Transportation, Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards) shall be installed in all motor vehicles.

notes.front: Under 1926.602, seat belts need not be provided for earthmoving equipment that has no {{c1::ROPS or adequate canopy protection}}.
notes.explanation: The exception sits in the seat-belt paragraph for earthmoving equipment, which otherwise requires belts on the equipment it covers.
notes.evidence: Seat belts need not be provided for equipment which does not have roll-over protective structure (ROPS) or adequate canopy protection.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.602(a)(2)(iii), Earthmoving equipment: seat belts, p. 333

notes.front: When must vehicles in use be checked under 1926.601, and what must happen to any defect found?
notes.back: At the beginning of each shift; all defects must be corrected before the vehicle is placed in service.
notes.explanation: The check covers parts such as service and parking brakes, tyres, horn, steering, coupling devices, seat belts, controls and safety devices, among others.
notes.evidence: All vehicles in use shall be checked at the beginning of each shift to assure that the following parts, equipment, and accessories are in safe operating condition and free of apparent damage that could cause failure while in use

notes.front: In the cranes and derricks standard, what is the fall zone?
notes.back: The area, including but not limited to the area directly beneath the load, where partially or completely suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident.
notes.explanation: The fall zone is wider than the footprint under the load: it covers wherever the materials could reasonably foreseeably land.
notes.evidence: Fall zone means the area (including but not limited to the area directly beneath the load) in which it is reasonably foreseeable that partially or completely suspended materials could fall in the event of an accident.

notes.front: While the operator is not moving a suspended load, which employees may be within the fall zone?
notes.back: Those hooking, unhooking or guiding the load; those making the initial attachment to a component or structure; those operating a concrete hopper or bucket.
notes.explanation: Everyone else must stay out of the fall zone under 1926.1425(b); where available, hoisting routes that minimise exposure to hoisted loads must also be used.
notes.evidence: While the operator is not moving a suspended load, no employee must be within the fall zone, except for employees: (1) Engaged in hooking, unhooking or guiding a load; (2) Engaged in the initial attachment of the load to a component or structure; or (3) Operating a concrete hopper or concrete bucket.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.1425(b), Keeping clear of the load, p. 702

notes.front: A crane holds a bundle of steel joists still above a deck. Four workers are nearby. Who may be inside the fall zone?
notes.choices:
A) The electrician taking a shortcut to the site hut
B) The surveyor checking levels under the bundle
C) The worker guiding the bundle with a tag line
D) The supervisor watching from beneath the bundle
notes.back: C: the worker guiding the bundle.
notes.choicesExplained: B, A and D are not hooking, unhooking or guiding the load, making its initial attachment, or operating a concrete hopper or bucket, so they must stay out.
notes.explanation: Guiding a load is one of the three activities 1926.1425(b) allows inside the fall zone while the load is not being moved.
notes.evidence: While the operator is not moving a suspended load, no employee must be within the fall zone, except for employees: (1) Engaged in hooking, unhooking or guiding a load
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.1425(b), Keeping clear of the load, p. 702

notes.front: What must trucks with dump bodies be equipped with, to stop the body lowering during maintenance or inspection?
notes.back: A positive means of support, permanently attached and capable of being locked in position.
notes.explanation: Section 1926.601(b)(10) states the purpose: preventing accidental lowering of the body while maintenance or inspection work is being done.
notes.evidence: Trucks with dump bodies shall be equipped with positive means of support, permanently attached, and capable of being locked in position to prevent accidental lowering of the body while maintenance or inspection work is being done.

notes.front: Bulldozer and scraper blades, end-loader buckets and dump bodies must be either {{c1::fully lowered or blocked}} when being repaired or when not in use.
notes.explanation: Section 1926.600(a)(3) adds that controls go to neutral, with motors stopped and brakes set, unless the work being performed requires otherwise.
notes.evidence: Bulldozer and scraper blades, end-loader buckets, dump bodies, and similar equipment, shall be either fully lowered or blocked when being repaired or when not in use.

notes.front: How large is the limited access zone for a masonry wall under construction, and on which side does it go?
notes.back: The wall's height plus four feet, along the wall's entire length, on the unscaffolded side.
notes.explanation: The zone must be set up before construction of the wall starts, and only employees actively engaged in building the wall may enter it.
notes.evidence: The limited access zone shall be equal to the height of the wall to be constructed plus four feet, and shall run the entire length of the wall. (3) The limited access zone shall be established on the side of the wall which will be unscaffolded.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.706(a), Requirements for masonry construction, p. 379

notes.front: A crew will build a block wall 12 feet high, scaffolded on its north face only. How wide must the limited access zone be, and where?
notes.choices:
A) 12 feet, on the north side
B) 8 feet, on either side
C) 16 feet, on the north side
D) 16 feet, on the south side
notes.back: D: 16 feet, on the south side.
notes.choicesExplained: A uses the height alone and the scaffolded side. C has the right width on the wrong side. B is too narrow and ignores which side is unscaffolded.
notes.explanation: The zone equals the wall height plus four feet (12 + 4 = 16) and goes on the side that will be unscaffolded.
notes.evidence: The limited access zone shall be equal to the height of the wall to be constructed plus four feet, and shall run the entire length of the wall. (3) The limited access zone shall be established on the side of the wall which will be unscaffolded.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.706(a), Requirements for masonry construction, p. 379

notes.front: All protruding reinforcing steel onto and into which employees could fall must be guarded to eliminate the hazard of {{c1::impalement}}.
notes.explanation: Section 1926.701(b) ties the duty to where employees could fall onto or into the steel, not to every bar on site.
notes.evidence: All protruding reinforcing steel, onto and into which employees could fall, shall be guarded to eliminate the hazard of impalement.

notes.front: Vertical rebar sticks up from a footing directly below a walkway where workers carry formwork. What does 1926.701 require?
notes.choices:
A) Guarding of the rebar to eliminate the impalement hazard
B) Nothing until the concrete is poured
C) A sign warning workers to watch their step
D) Painting the bar ends a bright colour
notes.back: A: guard the rebar to eliminate the impalement hazard.
notes.choicesExplained: C and D warn but do not guard, and the rule requires guarding. B is wrong: the duty applies while employees could fall onto the steel.
notes.explanation: Workers on the walkway could fall onto the protruding steel, which is exactly the situation 1926.701(b) covers.
notes.evidence: All protruding reinforcing steel, onto and into which employees could fall, shall be guarded to eliminate the hazard of impalement.

notes.front: What must be installed and maintained on pneumatic impact (percussion) tools, and why?
notes.back: Safety clips or retainers, to prevent attachments from being accidentally expelled.
notes.explanation: The purpose is stated in 1926.302(b)(2) itself; a separate paragraph requires the tool to be secured to its hose by some positive means.
notes.evidence: Safety clips or retainers shall be securely installed and maintained on pneumatic impact (percussion) tools to prevent attachments from being accidentally expelled.

notes.front: A demolition worker notices that the retaining clip on a pneumatic chipping hammer is missing, so the chisel bit is held only by friction. What does 1926.302 require before use?
notes.choices:
A) Wrap the bit with tape to hold it in
B) Install a safety clip or retainer on the tool
C) Use it only for short bursts
D) Lower the air pressure and carry on
notes.back: B: install a safety clip or retainer.
notes.choicesExplained: A, D and C leave the attachment free to be expelled; the rule requires a securely installed clip or retainer.
notes.explanation: A chipping hammer is a pneumatic impact tool, and 1926.302(b)(2) requires a clip or retainer on it so the attachment cannot be accidentally expelled.
notes.evidence: Safety clips or retainers shall be securely installed and maintained on pneumatic impact (percussion) tools to prevent attachments from being accidentally expelled.

notes.front: Compressed air may be used for cleaning only when reduced to less than {{c1::30}} psi, and then only with effective chip guarding and personal protective equipment.
notes.explanation: Both conditions apply together in 1926.302(b)(4): the reduced pressure alone is not enough.
notes.evidence: Compressed air shall not be used for cleaning purposes except where reduced to less than 30 p.s.i. and then only with effective chip guarding and personal protective equipment

notes.front: Who may operate a powder-actuated tool?
notes.back: Only employees trained in the operation of the particular tool in use.
notes.explanation: The training must match the tool in use, and 1926.302(e) also requires the tool to be tested each day before loading.
notes.evidence: Only employees who have been trained in the operation of the particular tool in use shall be allowed to operate a powderactuated tool.

notes.front: A carpenter trained on one make of powder-actuated tool is handed a different model the site has just bought. Under 1926.302(e), may the carpenter use it?
notes.choices:
A) Yes, if the tool passed its daily test
B) Yes, because any powder-actuated training counts
C) Yes, if a trained colleague watches
D) Not until trained in the operation of that particular tool
notes.back: D: not until trained on that particular tool.
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the training must be on the particular tool in use. C is not an exception in the rule. A is a separate requirement and does not replace training.
notes.explanation: The rule limits operation to employees trained on the particular tool in use, so training on another model does not qualify.
notes.evidence: Only employees who have been trained in the operation of the particular tool in use shall be allowed to operate a powderactuated tool.
